section: The values and principles of the UK
explanation: Democracy is one of the fundamental principles of British life, meaning government by the people through elected representatives.

angles.q: What does democracy mean?
angles.a: Government by the people, through elected representatives

angles.q: Which of these is a fundamental principle of British life?

section: The values and principles of the UK
explanation: The rule of law means that everyone, including those in government, is subject to the law and no one is above it.

angles.q: Under the rule of law, who is subject to the law?
wrong: Only people born in the UK
Only those who have been convicted

section: The values and principles of the UK
explanation: Individual liberty is a fundamental principle of British life, meaning people are free to make their own choices within the law.

angles.q: What does individual liberty mean?
angles.a: Freedom to make your own choices within the law

section: The values and principles of the UK
explanation: Tolerance of those with different faiths and beliefs is a fundamental principle of British life.

angles.q: Tolerance in British life extends to people with different what?

section: The values and principles of the UK
explanation: Participation in community life is a fundamental principle, and includes volunteering, voting and helping neighbours.

angles.q: Which of these is an example of participation in community life?

section: The values and principles of the UK
explanation: Respecting and obeying the law is the first of the responsibilities expected of everyone living in the UK.

angles.q: What is expected of everyone living in the UK regarding the law?
wrong: To obey only laws they agree with
To follow the laws of their home country

section: The values and principles of the UK
explanation: Looking after yourself and your family is one of the responsibilities expected of everyone living in the UK.

angles.q: Which of these is a listed responsibility of UK residents?
angles.a: Looking after yourself and your family

section: The values and principles of the UK
explanation: Looking after the area in which you live and the environment is one of the responsibilities of UK residents.

angles.q: Which of these shows responsibility towards the environment?

section: The values and principles of the UK
explanation: Freedom of speech is one of the rights shared by everyone in the UK, within the limits set by the law.

angles.q: Freedom of speech in the UK is subject to what?
angles.a: The limits set by the law

section: The values and principles of the UK
explanation: A right to a fair trial is one of the rights shared by everyone in the UK.

angles.q: Which of these rights is shared by everyone in the UK?
angles.a: A right to a fair trial
wrong: A right to choose your own judge
A right to a jury of your friends

section: The values and principles of the UK
explanation: A right to join in the election of a government is one of the rights shared by everyone eligible in the UK.

angles.q: Which of these rights is shared by eligible people in the UK?
angles.a: The right to join in electing a government
wrong: The right to appoint the Prime Minister
The right to choose the monarch

section: The values and principles of the UK
explanation: The UK offers a welcome to those who share its values, but does not tolerate extremism or intolerance.

angles.q: How does the UK treat extremism?
wrong: It protects it as free speech

explanation: To apply for permanent residence or citizenship, applicants must be able to speak and read English and understand life in the UK.

angles.q: Which two things must citizenship applicants demonstrate?
angles.a: English language ability and knowledge of life in the UK
wrong: A university degree and a sponsor

explanation: ESOL courses help people whose first language is not English to improve their English for settlement and citizenship.

angles.q: Who are ESOL courses designed for?
angles.a: People whose first language is not English
wrong: People learning a second European language

explanation: UK Visas and Immigration, part of the Home Office, handles applications to come to, remain in, or become a citizen of the UK.

angles.q: Which body handles applications for British citizenship?
wrong: The Department for Work and Pensions

explanation: At a citizenship ceremony, new citizens make a pledge to respect the rights, freedoms and laws of the UK.

angles.q: What does the citizenship pledge commit new citizens to respect?
angles.a: The rights, freedoms and laws of the UK
wrong: The policies of the governing party

section: Taking the Life in the UK Test
explanation: The Life in the UK Test must be booked in advance and taken at a registered test centre, where identification is required.

angles.q: What must you bring to a Life in the UK Test centre?

section: Taking the Life in the UK Test
explanation: All questions in the Life in the UK Test are based on the official handbook, Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents.

angles.q: The Life in the UK Test questions are based on what?
angles.a: The official handbook for new residents

explanation: The UK is made up of four countries: England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.

angles.q: Which of these is one of the four countries of the UK?

explanation: Great Britain refers to England, Scotland and Wales. The UK also includes Northern Ireland.

angles.q: Which three countries make up Great Britain?

explanation: Edinburgh is the capital of Scotland, and the Scottish Parliament sits there at Holyrood.

angles.q: Of which country is Edinburgh the capital?

explanation: Belfast is the capital of Northern Ireland and the seat of the Northern Ireland Assembly.

angles.q: What is the capital city of Northern Ireland?

explanation: Cardiff is the capital of Wales and the home of the Welsh Parliament, the Senedd.

angles.q: What is the capital city of Wales?

explanation: The currency of the UK is the pound sterling. There are 100 pence in a pound.

angles.q: What is the currency of the UK called?

explanation: Scotland and Northern Ireland issue their own banknotes, which are valid throughout the UK though shops elsewhere may not accept them.

angles.q: Which parts of the UK issue their own banknotes?

explanation: The Union Flag combines the crosses of St George, St Andrew and St Patrick. Wales is not represented on it.

angles.q: Whose cross on the Union Flag represents Scotland?
Whose cross on the Union Flag represents England?

explanation: The flag of Wales shows a red dragon. Wales is not represented on the Union Flag because it was already united with England.

angles.q: Which creature appears on the flag of Wales?

explanation: Gaelic is spoken in parts of Scotland, particularly the Highlands and Islands.

angles.q: In which part of Scotland is Gaelic most spoken?

explanation: Welsh is taught in schools in Wales and is used on road signs and official documents alongside English.

angles.q: Where in Wales would you see the Welsh language used officially?
angles.a: On road signs and official documents

explanation: British overseas territories include St Helena and the Falkland Islands. They are not part of the UK.

angles.q: Which of these is a British overseas territory?

explanation: The Isle of Man and the Channel Islands are Crown dependencies with their own governments, and are not part of the UK.

angles.q: The Isle of Man has what relationship to the UK?
angles.a: It is a Crown dependency, not part of the UK
wrong: It is a county of England
It is a fifth country of the UK
It is a British overseas territory

explanation: Northern Ireland is the only part of the UK with a land border with another country, the Republic of Ireland.

angles.q: With which country does Northern Ireland share a land border?

explanation: The UK Parliament sits at Westminster in London and governs the whole of the UK.

angles.q: In which part of London does the UK Parliament sit?
